  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
# Aroha

Aroha was sixty-six when she came to the clinic, her appointment card held carefully in both hands as though it might dissolve. She had worked as a network engineer for thirty-four years, a career built on precision and control—the kind of work that suited her temperament. She had been widowed for eleven years, lived alone in a modest house in suburban Portland, and had maintained a tight circle of professional colleagues and one longtime friend. Until three years ago, that life had held a kind of equilibrium.

The assault had happened on an evening in late autumn. Aroha had stayed late at the office to troubleshoot a server migration, a task she preferred to do after hours when the office was quiet. She had always felt safe there. When she left at nine o'clock, the parking garage was nearly empty. A man had emerged from behind a concrete pillar as she walked toward her car. She had not heard him approach. He had been drinking—she remembered the smell of whiskey on his breath, thick and sharp, overwhelming everything else—and he had grabbed her from behind with one arm around her throat. The other hand held a box cutter. She had felt the blade against her ribs, had felt the specific pressure of it through her blouse. She had not screamed. She had frozen, her mind fragmenting into the sensation of her own helplessness, the absolute certainty that whatever happened next was beyond her control.

The assault lasted seven minutes. It felt like hours.

When it was over, she had driven herself to the hospital. She had reported it to the police. She had done all the things one is supposed to do. But in the months that followed, something had shifted in how she inhabited her own body and her own world.

The smell of alcohol now triggered an immediate panic response. She had begun to notice weapons everywhere—the letter opener on her desk at work, the chef's knife visible through the glass of her kitchen cabinet, the decorative letter opener her friend Maria had given her years ago, which she now kept in a drawer because she could not bear to see it. At the grocery store, she found herself tracking the position of every person holding a cart or basket, assessing which items could be used as instruments. These observations were constant, automatic, and exhausting. What frightened her most was that even when her rational mind knew she was safe—she was in her own home, the doors were locked, no one was there—she could not make herself believe it. The knowledge and the feeling never aligned.

In the first year after the assault, Aroha had withdrawn from the few social connections that remained. When Maria had tried to hug her at a coffee shop, Aroha's entire nervous system had ignited. She had flinched so violently that she had knocked over her cup. The physical recoil had been involuntary, but the shame had not. She had come to avoid any situation where someone might touch her unexpectedly, and then gradually, any situation where emotional closeness might lead to physical contact at all. She had declined dinner invitations. She had stopped attending the monthly book club she had enjoyed. She had begun to eat very little, carefully rationing her meals, counting calories, finding in the restriction a small pocket of control that extended beyond her actual reach.

At work, her performance had begun to slip. She had always been meticulous, but now she found herself unable to concentrate during meetings. When a junior engineer had placed a hand on her shoulder to show her something on her screen, Aroha had startled so violently that she had knocked over her coffee. She had apologized, but the incident had marked a boundary. Her colleagues had begun to treat her with a kind of careful distance. She had taken early leave from a major project, citing fatigue. The truth was more complicated: she had come to feel that she had betrayed something essential about herself by freezing, by not fighting, by surviving in a way that had left her feeling complicit in her own violation.

Three months ago, Maria had finally insisted. She had told Aroha that she barely recognized her anymore, that the woman who had once loved hiking and cooking and late-night conversations had disappeared. Maria had said this gently, but it had landed hard. Aroha had realized that she was not truly living—she was merely enduring, moving through days in a state of constant vigilance, cut off from the few people who cared about her, convinced that her body was no longer her own and that the world was a place where terrible things happened to people who were powerless to stop them.

It was Maria's words that had finally brought her to the clinic door. Aroha wanted to believe that she could reclaim something of her life, but she was not certain it was possible. What she feared most was that she would have to feel, truly feel, what had been done to her—and that even then, she would still be broken.
